title: print() displays the current value on the screen
when_to_show: When predicting the output of `print()` or following the execution order of multi-line code
body: print() is a function that displays the value inside the parentheses on the screen. When reading code, it serves as a reference point for checking what the calculated value is up to the current line.
detail: Python code executes line by line from top to bottom, unless there are special conditional statements or loops. Therefore, if a variable’s value has changed before `print()` is called, the output will reflect the updated value. If there are quotation marks, as in `print("name")`, the string “name” is printed exactly as written; if there are no quotation marks, as in `print(name)`, the value stored in the variable `name` is retrieved and printed.

title: Output prediction follows all lines preceding the `print` statement.
when_to_show: When tracking changes in variable values in a problem involving selecting output results
body: It’s easy to get the output prediction problem wrong if you solve it by looking only at the last `print` line.
detail: `print` doesn’t suddenly generate a value on that line; rather, it displays on the screen values that have already been stored and calculated in previous lines. Therefore, you must first check what values have been assigned to the variables and then trace the flow to see if those values are copied to other variables or recalculated. If a value is assigned to the same variable multiple times, the value stored last is used in subsequent lines.

title: A variable is a label used to track a value.
when_to_show: When reading code in which a value is stored in a variable or the value of the same variable is changed again
body: A variable is a name assigned to a value so that it can be referenced later. “x = 3” means that the name “x” now refers to the value 3.
detail: If you assign a new value to the same variable—such as “x = 5”—the code will use the new value, 5, from that point on. Therefore, when reading a problem involving variables, it’s safest to write down the variable’s current value on each line. A common mistake beginners make is confusing the variable name itself with the value it holds.

title: In college entrance exams, you calculate the right side and then store the result on the left.
when_to_show: When reading code that updates the value of the same variable, such as `x = x + 1`,
body: In assignment, the right-hand side is evaluated first, and the result is then stored in the variable on the left.
detail: For example, `x = x + 1` might seem strange, but the expression first reads the previous value of `x` from the right-hand side, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. Therefore, the value of a variable can change over time. When reading code, if the same variable name appears multiple times, you shouldn’t just remember the initial value; you must continuously update your understanding of what the new value is after each line is executed.

title: If there are quotation marks, read it literally
when_to_show: When distinguishing between strings and variable names that look similar
body: In Python, a value enclosed in quotes is a string. Since a string is a literal value, "name" is a four-character string, not code that searches for the variable `name`.
detail: Conversely, "name" without quotes is interpreted as a variable name. If you write `print(name)` after `name = "Python"`, "Python" is printed, but if you write `print("name")`, the word "name" is printed. This distinction is a very common source of errors in beginner-level output prediction problems.

title: String numbers and actual numbers are different.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between the results of calculations involving numbers with quotation marks and those without
body: Even though they look similar on the screen, '3' and 3 are different values. '3' is a string, and 3 is a number.
detail: When you add two strings together, it’s concatenation, not arithmetic, so '3' + '4' becomes '34'. When you add two numbers together, it’s arithmetic, so 3 + 4 equals 7. A common mistake beginners make is assuming that two values are the same just because they look the same on the screen.

title: Basic errors often occur with names, quotation marks, and indentation.
when_to_show: When reading about common runtime errors and syntax errors in beginner-level code
body: Beginners often make mistakes in basic syntax rather than with complex algorithms. If you use a variable like `print(name)` before declaring it, you may get a `NameError`.
detail: Failing to close the quotation marks around a string can result in a SyntaxError. If the indentation is incorrect in code following a colon—such as in `if` or `for` statements—an IndentationError may occur. Error messages may look intimidating, but they usually contain hints about the line where the problem occurred or its cause.

title: Basic grammar is the backbone of real-world code.
when_to_show: When explaining how the beginner-level grammar cards relate to actual project code,
body: Basic syntax elements—such as print, variables, strings, and numbers—aren’t just used in small examples.
detail: Real-world project code ultimately follows the same flow: storing values, calculating necessary values, and outputting the results to the screen or a file. Code that reads data files must distinguish between strings and numbers, and web app code also processes user-entered values as variables. Therefore, even though the beginner-level cards may seem like simple problems, they form the foundation for reading real-world code.
